North Carolina, and about 3.7 miles northeast of the Bad Creek site. The Bearcamp Creek site is located within the Nantahala National Forest. The lower reservoir would be Lake Jocassee.
The upper reservoir would contain 80,000 acre-feet of usable storage between water surface elevations of 1,730 and 1,570 feet. At maximum elevation (1,730 feet), this reservoir would have a surface area of 520 acres. The dam would be 350 feet high with a crest length of about 1,700 feet. The power tunnel would have a length of 4,200 feet and would be 37 feet in diameter. Because of the relatively short length of the waterway, the powerhouse would probably be a surface type located on the bank of the Jocassee Lake.
8.3.2.1 Flora
Vegetation of the Bearcamp Creek area is very similar to that described in Subsection 2.2.1. The three major communities are oak-hickory (on the slopes), pine (on the dry ridges), and tulip poplar and other hardwoods (in the coves). Most of the forest is second growth due to extensive lumbering activities in the area. Pines, oaks, hickories, beech, hemlock, basswood, black locust, and dogwood have all been harvested at one time or another (Rodgers and Shake, 1965). Logging operations opened up the canopy and favored the establishment of pines and poplars, but hindered the establishment of other types of trees.
Impacts would be very similar to those discussed for the proposed Bad Creek site in Subsections 3.1.2 and 3.2.2. The upper reservoir would inundate more vegetation than any of the other alternative sites - 520 acres. Dr. Leland Rodgers has suggested that the Upper Falls of Bearcamp Creek should receive protective status (Bruce and Pittillo, 1974). He mentioned that it was an important Shortia galacifolia (endangered) habitat.
8.3.2.2 Fauna
Detailed information regarding the fish and wildlife resources of the Bearcamp Creek site is unavailable, but it is likely that wildlife habitat and wildlife populations at or near the site are similar to those for the Bad Creek area. Signs of bear and other wildlife were noted at the nearby Coley Creek site, and the area has been described as having a remote wildland character (Dysart, et al., 1973).
